From kilts in Scotland to tunics in Rome and from hills to skirts. Fashion Was Once Fluid. But today it isn't. How did we go from a world of skirts and frogs to one of pants and shirts for men across the globe? And why does India tell one of the most fascinating versions of this story?

Let's start at the absolute beginning. Here is a Priest King wearing a patterned rope, stretching out from his shoulder, covering his entire body. He also wears two bands, one on his forehead, and one on his arm. R Rather Evidence: A figure in a seated couple shows both of them wearing nearly identical dresses with beads around the neck. We also have evidence of the earliest normal weave textile at Harappa. This impression suggests that it dates to somewhere around 3300 BCE.

Now This Is The Most Interesting Period In Clothing History. Curiously, the Harappans left us textiles, but the Vedic period left us almost none. The only evidence we found was from a poem in the Rigveda which mentions the word cloth in it. If we look at the paintings of the Mahabharata, they show men wearing posh or single layered ropes. The Mauryas stitch a new vocabulary into fashion Antariya and Uttariya Antariya represented lower body clothing and Uttariya represented upper body clothing The Mauryas introduce structure to clothing with a waist band called the kayabandh A small resemblance of tightness and distinction in clothing. Clothing shifted from pure drape to partial structures while maintaining that waviness. Similar to the band on the west, a band called Pratidhi was

introduced for women to cover their breasts. Another distinction was noticed in the boots of soldiers. As they are stretched to knee length, this is probably done for extra protection in the harsh terrain of battle.  Before the expansion of the Gupta Empire, there was a time in history when Central Asian rulers controlled the northern part of India and with their rule, they also brought an entire wardrobe to share. Their fashion was divided into three

parts. A calf length, over code called, the chhuga. An open kurta, a KA tunic, and baggy trousers tugged into booths called driving. They also carried Roman influence in their clothing and had these Frankish designs to wear at the bottom giving a new form of babyness to the clothes. Their Roman influence leaks into the kind of shots they wore which is the most distinct part about Roman soldiers.

The Gupta era polished it all with the adoption of stitched garments and richer fabrics. The men's fashion landscape  saw a visible turn toward more meticulously designed clothes. The body still remains an integral part, but it was a class that brought the difference. S  Different classes and sectors of society adopted different forms of clothing. Fabric becomes the language of what you do in society. This time period saw minimal changes in the Indian clothing landscape. Banab Bhatta

Rot about the costume of King Harsha wearing a dhoti and a scarf decorated with gusset patterns. Alberuni a traveller also mentions that kurtaka and shalwar in his book Tariq ul Hind the skirtish nature of clothing still remain during this time period. But now it was time for a change. Until now the common theme has been that every time a ruler changed  the clothing change to this era was no different but with an

exception traveller Ibin Haukal noted that in areas like Multan and Sindh the Muslims and infidels in this region wore the same dress and let their beards grow in the same fashion. They use fine muslin garments on account of the extreme heat. All wear short uniforms except the merchants who wear shirts and clothes of cotton like the men of Iraq and Persia. During the onset of the Delhi Sultanate, a long, loose-fitting robe with a straight cut, worn

with a sash and belt around the waist, was worn by both the elite and middle classes and was known as the jubba. Apart from this, the Mughals adopted Indian attire which was similar to the jama that was the Rajput war and angarka churidar pyjama and a kamar bandh. The weather conditions of India made the Jama a favourable piece. The ruffles in the churidar pyjama and the open-frock structure helped with air circulation which kept the

body cool throughout the scorching heat. But there was one small detail about Jamaaz which changed its entire meaning. The flap, the direction in which the flap was folded conveyed your identity. Hindus fold to the left where as Muslims do it on the right. Dior's clothes also came into Vogue during this period. So delicate that the body beneath shows, creating a translucent look. The turban also remains an integral part of Indian men's clothing.

To the extent that anyone without one was considered inauspicious. Angka Which Translates to One That Protects  The Lims A Lighter and Shorter Version of the Jama Started to Gain Popularity. It wraps just above the waist and is known to be knee length. Wear s the Jama Wood Wrap Around the Chest.  The frock structure of clothing went from being fitted in the interior to the northern as loose

pajamas took the place of lower garments  Especially in North West India then came the Industrial Revolution and the mass production of textiles began  Indian weaving was slowly being replaced by the ease of mass produced  clothes which would get widely used throughout the country. The British entry played a part  in it as they didn't just want to rule India but also wanted to dress India through propaganda and education. The masses were subtly introduced into

adopting Western, tight-fitted clothes. British fashion was also fused with Indian fashion to make them more easily adoptable by Indians. The Achkan, a fitted garment like an English coat but slimmer and tighter  which was derived from the Chapkan and Angka became a norm for the elites.  During this time, sherwanis were also invented and became mainstream formal wear, and buttons were slowly getting integrated into every form of

clothing.  But even through these changes, the turbans never lost their essence and place their role in indoor men's fashion. But during this period fashion mostly focused on their elite  and upper class. S The middle and lower classes were still wearing native clothes. Thanks to Gandhi. The trend of gaadi  and simpler clothing influenced the masses and self-woven material also played a key role in appealing to the lower class people as they were mostly

employed as craftsmen. For the upper  class any traditional tunic has seemingly got replaced by a kurta and achkan remain the formal wear while the dhoti still remains prevalent. More Over By This Time The Flowy Webby Nature Of Clothes Was Almost Gone  And No Skirtish Structure Remains. Even when India gains independence, the emphasis on national identity is put over through every idea of British symbolism, even in closing. But this didn't continue for too long. The

effects of modernization and the global economy began to  take hold in India in the 1960s where waste and clothing dominated in urban areas. With the onset of the 21st century, India opened its doors  to global markets and the liberalization of the Indian economy  attracted international brands to set up their presence in India. The market  expanded quickly with the support of media and television which now has abandoned that which was more functional for the hot

climate of India and has evolved over centuries. It was abandoned as a symbol of the poor making pants a status symbol. The perceived value of pants and shirts made them more appealing than the utility of dos and any other native tunics. Slowly Bringing the Change Across Generations.
